question.problem:
Calculate 
${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+5n+6}.$

*Hint: Try to factor the denominator first.*
question.worked_solution:
First, factoring the denominator and using partial fractions, we can write the series as

$$
\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+5n+6}=\frac{1}{(n+2)(n+3)}=\frac{1}{n+2}-\frac{1}{n+3}.
$$

So, our series can be written as

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }(\frac{1}{n+2}-\frac{1}{n+3}).
$$

Let's now compute the first few partial sums:

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}_{1} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\ {s}_{2} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\frac{1}{5}) \\ {s}_{3} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{5}}-\frac{1}{6}) \\ {s}_{4} & =(\frac{1}{3}-\cancel{\frac{1}{4}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{4}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{5}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{5}}-\cancel{\frac{1}{6}})+(\cancel{\frac{1}{6}}-\frac{1}{7})\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that for each partial sum, we always end up canceling all terms except for the first and last terms. Therefore, the $N$th partial sum is

$$
{s}_{N}=\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{N+3}.
$$

Finally, we can determine the sum of the series by taking the limit of ${s}_{N}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(n+2)(n+3)} & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }{s}_{N} \\  & ={lim}_{N\to \infty }(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{N+3}) \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
